proof:
# Adaptive pairing with arbitrary endpoint shapes and a simplex middle fiber

Let A,K,B be compact convex planar bodies of areas a,k,b>0. Suppose

    (A+B)/2 subset K, a=k+b,

and suppose K is a simplex. Regard them as fibers at integer coordinates
-1,0,1, with mixed volume measure mu equal to planar area on each fiber.
Let H_0,H_1,H_2 be any three closed ambient halfspaces whose middle
traces are the three centroid facet caps of K, namely lambda_i>=1/3.
Then the quantitative bound is

    sum_i mu(H_i)>=4a/3+min(2b/3,k/27)>4a/3.      (1)

The integer coefficients of the halfspaces may be arbitrary. In
particular all oblique extensions of these three middle traces are
covered by (1). The endpoint bodies need not be homothetic or have
any symmetry.

## 1. Every right source point has enough good left neighbors

Let D be the set in K covered by at least two of its centroid facet
caps. For each y in B the convex set

    Q_y=(A+y)/2

lies in K and has area a/4. The sharp signed-area theorem proved in
`candidate c5127f255244bd3c` gives

    |Q_y|-3|Q_y intersect D|<=2k/9.

Undoing the dilation gives the exact good-neighbor capacity

    |{x in A:(x+y)/2 in D}|
      =4|Q_y intersect D|
      >=a/3-8k/27
      =b/3+k/27=:c_*.                            (2)

In particular c_*>b/3. This is a proved convex-subset inequality, not
an assumed existence of an optimally shaped target law.

## 2. Attained capacity matching and cap multiplicity

The relation G={(x,y) in A x B:(x+y)/2 in D} is closed. The attained
capacity-matching lemma in `candidate fbf10959836f7b72`
provides a nonnegative measure pi on G with marginals dominated by
unit Lebesgue density on A and B and mass at least min(b,c_*).
For completeness, its proof takes a maximum-mass feasible measure by
weak compactness. If its mass g is below min(b,c_*), its residual
marginals alpha,beta have alpha(G_y)>=c_*-g, so the positive measure
1_G(alpha x beta), after a sufficiently small scaling, can be added to
it. This contradicts maximality. Thus the matching is proved to exist
and its maximum mass is attained.

Since a>=b, complete this partial matching to a coupling Pi of all of
unit Lebesgue measure on B and a submeasure bounded by unit density on
A, using a scaled product of the residual marginals. The total mass of
Pi is b. Every midpoint belongs to K and hence lies in at least one
centroid facet cap. The good matching lies in at least two. Writing N
for this multiplicity,

    integral N((x+y)/2)dPi
       >=b+min(b,c_*)>4b/3.                      (3)

Strictness follows because b>0 and both b and c_* exceed b/3.

## 3. Transfer to the actual ambient cap masses

For each closed halfspace H_i, the affine midpoint identity implies
pointwise

    1_Hi(0,(x+y)/2)
       <=1_Hi(-1,x)+1_Hi(1,y).

Integrate against Pi. The source marginal bounds give

    sum_i [|A intersect (H_i)_{-1}|+|B intersect (H_i)_1|]
       >=integral N((x+y)/2)dPi.

Each middle centroid facet cap has area gamma_2 k=4k/9, so adding
their total middle contribution 4k/3 and using (3) proves (1). More
precisely, subtracting 4a/3 gives the exact certified margin
min(2b/3,k/27). Consequently one of these caps has mass at least
gamma_2 a+min(2b/9,k/81).

The total three-fiber mass is M=a+k+b=2a. Therefore these three ambient
caps cannot all have mass below gamma_2 M/2. If b=0 and a=k, each
prescribed middle cap already has that mass, so the analogous
impossibility of three strictly smaller caps follows directly.

## Exact remaining scope

This theorem controls a particular three-cap family: the middle fiber
must be a simplex, and its three traces must be its centroid facet
caps. An arbitrary certificate of low halfspace depth may instead
involve different orientations, different thresholds, more cap groups,
or a non-simplex middle fiber. Neither the signed-area theorem nor
(1) supplies a deformation replacing such a certificate by these
three prescribed traces while preserving every total cap-mass bound.
The argument also does not prove that the middle centroid has the
desired depth against every single halfspace. Thus it is a complete
auxiliary finite-cover theorem in its stated class, not an OC proof.
